subsection: CO₂ as a controlling factor in plant stomata

notes.h: The effect of CO₂ concentration on stomata (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Stomata are the tiny pores in a leaf's surface through which CO₂ enters and water vapour escapes. Their width is not fixed: the plant adjusts it in response to several signals, and the concentration of CO₂ inside the leaf is one of them.
points: The concentration of CO₂ in the air spaces inside the leaf (the gaps between the cells) is one of the factors that controls the width of the stomatal pores, along with light and water supply.
A low concentration of CO₂ inside the leaf causes the stomata to open, or to open wider, so that more CO₂ can diffuse in.
A high concentration of CO₂ inside the leaf causes the stomata to close, or partly close, so less gas passes through the pore.
Each stoma is surrounded by two guard cells, which change shape to open or close the pore. Guard cells respond to the CO₂ concentration around them, so the response is local to each stoma.
Low CO₂ leads to potassium ions (K⁺) being taken into the guard cells, water entering by osmosis and the guard cells becoming turgid (swollen and firm), so the pore opens.
High CO₂ leads to K⁺ leaving the guard cells, water following by osmosis and the guard cells becoming flaccid (limp), so the pore closes.

The response is to the concentration inside the leaf, which depends on the balance between photosynthesis, which uses CO₂, and respiration, which releases it. It is not simply the concentration in the outside air.
notes.tip: The direction is easily reversed: high CO₂ closes the stomata and low CO₂ opens them. Say that it is the CO₂ inside the leaf that matters, not the air outside, and name carbon dioxide as the gas when asked which gas affects stomatal diameter. There is more on the guard-cell mechanism in Transport of water and minerals.

notes.h: Why the response makes sense: day and night (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The CO₂ response is useful because the CO₂ level inside a leaf changes with the balance between photosynthesis and respiration, so the stomata open when CO₂ is needed and close when it is not.
points: In the light, photosynthesis uses CO₂ faster than respiration produces it, so the CO₂ concentration in the air spaces falls. The low CO₂ opens the stomata, letting in more CO₂ for photosynthesis exactly when it is needed.
In darkness there is no photosynthesis, but respiration continues, so CO₂ builds up in the air spaces. The high CO₂ closes the stomata.
The plant does not need CO₂ in the dark, so closing the stomata saves water that would otherwise be lost by transpiration (evaporation of water vapour through the open stomata).

This is a negative feedback loop (a change sets off a response that reverses the change). When internal CO₂ is low, the stomata open and CO₂ enters, so its concentration rises; as it rises, the stomata begin to close.

CO₂ concentration therefore helps match the opening of the stomata to the leaf's demand for CO₂, keeping the balance between taking in CO₂ and losing water. There is more on negative feedback in Homeostasis as a stimulus-response model.
The CO₂ response works together with the other controls. Light opens the stomata directly as well as by lowering CO₂ through photosynthesis.

Shortage of water closes the stomata even when CO₂ is low, because preventing wilting takes priority over photosynthesis. So on a hot, dry afternoon the stomata may close although the leaf needs CO₂, and photosynthesis slows.

Experimental evidence: if a leaf in the light is given air with extra CO₂, its stomata close partly. If a leaf in the dark is given CO₂-free air, its stomata open partly. This shows that CO₂ acts on the stomata on its own, separately from light.
notes.tip: If asked for the benefit to the plant of the stomatal response to CO₂, link the two halves: low CO₂ in the light opens the stomata for photosynthesis, and high CO₂ in the dark closes them to save water. Explain it through CO₂ inside the leaf falling in the light because of photosynthesis, not because the outside air has low CO₂.

notes.h: CO₂, stomata and transpiration (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Stomata are the main route by which a leaf loses water, so anything that changes their width also changes the rate of transpiration. This links CO₂ to water loss, and to wider questions about farming and climate.
points: Because CO₂ controls the width of the stomata, it affects transpiration. Raising the CO₂ concentration around a leaf closes the stomata partly and reduces the rate of transpiration; lowering it opens them and increases the rate.
This is why CO₂ concentration is one of the factors in Investigation: rate of transpiration.

Sustainability link: the CO₂ concentration of the atmosphere is rising, mainly from burning fossil fuels. Plants grown in raised CO₂ tend to open their stomata less, so they lose less water per unit of sugar made.
Leaves of the same species collected over the last two centuries and kept in herbarium collections (preserved plant specimens) show fewer stomata per unit area as CO₂ has risen.
Technology link: glasshouse growers add CO₂ to raise photosynthesis. The extra CO₂ also partly closes the stomata, so the plants lose less water.
notes.tip: State the effect of high or low CO₂ on the stomata first, then follow it through to the rate of transpiration. There is more on the experiment in Investigation: rate of photosynthesis.

notes.h: CO₂ as a controlling factor in plants and in humans compared (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Plants and humans both use CO₂ concentration to control gas exchange, but they respond in opposite ways. Comparing them shows that the difference comes from what CO₂ means to each organism.
points: What is detected, in plants: the CO₂ concentration inside the leaf, detected by the guard cells themselves. Plants have no nerves, so the response is local, in each stoma.

What is detected, in humans: the CO₂ concentration of the blood, through its effect on blood pH. Chemoreceptors (cells that detect chemical change) in the medulla oblongata and in the carotid and aortic bodies detect it and signal the breathing centre in the medulla.
Response to high CO₂: in plants the stomata close, reducing gas exchange. In humans the rate and depth of breathing increase, increasing gas exchange.
Response to low CO₂: in plants the stomata open. In humans breathing slows.

Why the responses are opposite, in plants: for a plant in the light, CO₂ is a raw material for photosynthesis, so low internal CO₂ signals that more is needed, and high internal CO₂ signals that none is being used, so water should be saved.
Why the responses are opposite, in humans: CO₂ is a waste product of respiration that makes the blood more acidic, so high CO₂ signals that more must be removed.
What is similar: in both, CO₂ concentration is the main controlling signal for gas exchange, and the control works by negative feedback, returning the CO₂ level towards normal.

In both, the controlled structures adjust how much gas passes across the exchange surface: the stomata in plants, and the diaphragm and intercostal muscles that ventilate the alveoli in humans. There is more on this in CO₂ as a controlling factor in breathing.
notes.tip: Questions ask you to outline the role of CO₂ in stomata and in breathing, and to compare them. Remember that in humans high CO₂ speeds breathing up, and never write that high CO₂ opens stomata to let it out. Give both the difference (opposite responses) and the similarity (negative feedback).

keyTerms.term: CO₂ as a controlling factor (Higher Level)
keyTerms.definition: The effect of the CO₂ concentration inside a leaf on the opening of its stomata: low CO₂ opens them and high CO₂ closes them.
A control in which a change in a variable triggers a response that reverses the change, returning the variable towards its normal level.
The loop in which low internal CO₂ opens the stomata, CO₂ enters and rises, and the rising CO₂ then makes the stomata begin to close.
A substance used up in a chemical reaction, such as CO₂ in photosynthesis.
A substance produced by a reaction that the body must remove, such as CO₂ from respiration.
A receptor that detects a chemical change, such as the rise in blood CO₂ in humans, and sends signals to the brain.
The part of the brainstem that contains the breathing centre, which increases the rate and depth of breathing when blood CO₂ rises.
A collection of preserved plant specimens, which can be used to compare leaves gathered over many years.

questions.prompt: State the effect of a high concentration of carbon dioxide inside a leaf on its stomata, and explain why the CO₂ concentration inside a leaf is usually high at night.
questions.model: A high concentration of CO₂ inside the leaf causes the stomata to close, or partly close. At night there is no photosynthesis to use CO₂, but respiration continues in every living cell and releases CO₂ into the air spaces of the leaf, so the concentration builds up. Closing the stomata at night saves water that would otherwise be lost by transpiration.

questions.prompt: Explain how changes in carbon dioxide concentration inside a leaf help to control the opening of stomata during the day, and describe this as a negative feedback loop.
questions.model: In the light, photosynthesis uses CO₂ faster than respiration produces it, so the CO₂ concentration in the leaf falls. Low CO₂ causes the stomata to open: K⁺ enters the guard cells, water follows by osmosis, the guard cells become turgid and the pore opens, letting more CO₂ in. As CO₂ enters and its concentration rises, the stomata begin to close. This is negative feedback, because the change in CO₂ produces a response that reverses the change. The supply of CO₂ is matched to the leaf's demand, while water loss is limited.

questions.prompt: Compare the role of carbon dioxide concentration as a controlling factor in plant stomata and in the human breathing system.
questions.model: In both plants and humans, CO₂ concentration is the main signal controlling gas exchange, and the control works by negative feedback that returns CO₂ towards normal. In plants, the guard cells detect the CO₂ concentration inside the leaf. Low CO₂ opens the stomata, and high CO₂ closes them, through the uptake and loss of K⁺ and the osmosis that follows. In humans, chemoreceptors in the medulla oblongata and in the carotid and aortic bodies detect the rise in blood CO₂, which lowers blood pH, and signal the breathing centre. High CO₂ increases the rate and depth of breathing, and low CO₂ slows it. The responses are opposite because CO₂ is a raw material for photosynthesis in plants, so low CO₂ means more is needed, whereas in humans it is a waste product of respiration that must be removed. In both, the controlled structures, the stomata or the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, adjust how much gas passes across the exchange surface.
